[![Image 1: This is a good article. Click here for more information.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/94/Symbol_support_vote.svg/20px-Symbol_support_vote.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Good_articles* "This is a good article. Click here for more information.")

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/71/Klein-development-math-19thcentury-english.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Klein-development-math-19thcentury-english.png)

Cover of _Development of Mathematics in The 19th Century_, by Felix Klein, translated from the German into English by M. Ackerman

**_Vorlesungen über die Entwicklung der Mathematik im 19. Jahrhundert_** (German for 'Lectures on the Development of Mathematics in the 19th Century') is a book by [Felix Klein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein "Felix Klein") that was published posthumously in two volumes (volumes 24 and 25 of [Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grundlehren_der_mathematischen_Wissenschaften&action=edit&redlink=1 "Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften (page does not exist)") ([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grundlehren_der_mathematischen_Wissenschaften "de:Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften"))) in 1926 and 1927.

Felix Klein had lectured on the development of mathematics in the 19th century and then on [relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theory_of_relativity "Theory of relativity") during World War I. The books were created from the notes of these lectures and edited by [Richard Courant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Courant "Richard Courant") and [Otto Neugebauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Neugebauer "Otto Neugebauer") for the first volume and Courant and [Stefan Cohn-Vossen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_Cohn-Vossen "Stefan Cohn-Vossen") for the second. Some content that Klein had originally envisioned as part of the text is missing.

The book has been enthusiastically received and widely praised. The first volume has been translated into Russian in 1937 and into English in 1979; in 1989, a second Russian translation appeared, followed in 2003 by a translation of the second volume. Both volumes have also been translated into Chinese.

Background and publication
--------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and publication")\]

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Max_Liebermann_Felix_Klein_1912.png/250px-Max_Liebermann_Felix_Klein_1912.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Max_Liebermann_Felix_Klein_1912.png)

Portrait of Felix Klein by [Max Liebermann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Liebermann "Max Liebermann"), 1912

[Felix Klein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein "Felix Klein") (1849–1925) was a German mathematician best known for his [Erlangen program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erlangen_program "Erlangen program"), which emphasised the use of [groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_/(mathematics/) "Group (mathematics)") in geometry. From 1886 to 1913 he was professor at the [University of Göttingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_G%C3%B6ttingen "University of Göttingen"), which became one of the leading centres of mathematical research under his leadership.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'ConnorRobertson2003-1)

Klein was interested in the history of mathematics and bought relevant books for the Göttingen library.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021479-2) One of his students, [Conrad Müller](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Conrad_M%C3%BCller&action=edit&redlink=1 "Conrad Müller (page does not exist)") ([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrad_M%C3%BCller "de:Conrad Müller")), studied for a PhD in history of mathematics under Klein and was later awarded the first [habilitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habilitation "Habilitation") degree in Göttingen in this topic area.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021479-2) Klein was responsible for the mathematical content in an encyclopaedic project called _[Die Kultur der Gegenwart](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Die_Kultur_der_Gegenwart&action=edit&redlink=1 "Die Kultur der Gegenwart (page does not exist)")_  ([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die_Kultur_der_Gegenwart "de:Die Kultur der Gegenwart")) ('The Culture of the Present') published by [B. G. Teubner Verlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._G._Teubner_Verlag "B. G. Teubner Verlag") ([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._G._Teubner_Verlag "de:B. G. Teubner Verlag")) in Leipzig, a publishing house he had longstanding ties with. The history of mathematics was supposed to be covered in three volumes; [H. G. Zeuthen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hieronymus_Georg_Zeuthen "Hieronymus Georg Zeuthen") was responsible for the period up to the middle ages and [Paul Stäckel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_St%C3%A4ckel "Paul Stäckel") for the time from 1500 to 1800. For covering 19th century applied mathematics, Klein tried to convince [Heinrich Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Martin_Weber "Heinrich Martin Weber") and [Carl Runge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Runge "Carl Runge"), but he eventually accepted he had to do it himself.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20203-3)

Klein planned to lecture on the development of mathematics in the 19th century in the winter semester of 1910/11 and again in the winter semester of 1912/13, but both times was unable to do so.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021480-4) The classes were then taught privately during World War I.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021537-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTECourantNeugebauer1979V-6) The winter 1914/15 courses were not announced in the _[Vorlesungsverzeichnis](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vorlesungsverzeichnis&action=edit&redlink=1 "Vorlesungsverzeichnis (page does not exist)")_  ([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungsverzeichnis "de:Vorlesungsverzeichnis")) (list of lectures), while the summer 1915 and winter 1915/16 courses were announced as "_privatissime_ and free of charge".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021537-5) The first semester of lectures was attended by 24 people, including 13 male students, 9 faculty and 2 women. The women were [Iris Runge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iris_Runge "Iris Runge") and Klein's daughter Elisabeth Staiger.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20203-3) The first two semesters of lecture notes were edited and typed by the recently widowed Staiger, while the third course was worked on by [Käthe Heinemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%A4the_Heinemann "Käthe Heinemann") and [Helene Stähelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helene_St%C3%A4helin "Helene Stähelin").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021537-5)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20204-7) Stähelin's part, completed in Basel in 1918, included figures drawn by [Erwin Voellmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erwin_Voellmy "Erwin Voellmy").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021537-5) For a few years, the lecture notes were only available as these typescripts.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20204-7) After Klein's death, [Richard Courant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Courant "Richard Courant") and [Otto Neugebauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Neugebauer "Otto Neugebauer") edited the notes and published the first volume in 1926 in the [Springer Verlag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springer_Science%2BBusiness_Media "Springer Science+Business Media")'s "yellow series", _[Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grundlehren_der_mathematischen_Wissenschaften&action=edit&redlink=1 "Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften (page does not exist)")_  ([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grundlehren_der_mathematischen_Wissenschaften "de:Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften")).[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTECourantNeugebauer1979V%E2%80%93VI-8)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021537-5) In their preface, they explained that they had changed as little as possible in the original text and admitted it was closer to a draft than to a thorough and balanced presentation of the history.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTECourantNeugebauer1979VI-9) While they thanked several other mathematicians for their help, they did not mention the three women who had prepared the typescripts from the original lectures anywhere in the book.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021537-5)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20204-7)

Possibly because the _Kultur der Gegenwart_ project was running into financial difficulties caused by the war, or because of his personal interests, Klein's lectures from 1916 onwards were concerned with relativity,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20204-7) and he postponed working on content regarding the works of [Poincaré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Poincar%C3%A9 "Henri Poincaré") and [Sophus Lie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophus_Lie "Sophus Lie").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20205-10) Starting in 1916, Klein taught his lectures in his own house to avoid having to walk to the university.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20204-7) The notes were taken by Klein's assistant [Walter Baade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Baade "Walter Baade").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20204-7) Klein's lectures on "selected aspects of newer mathematics" were concerned with [Einstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein "Albert Einstein"), the [special theory of relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_theory_of_relativity "Special theory of relativity") on an invariant basis, and the foundations of [general relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity "General relativity").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021535-11) In 1916, his audience of 14 included the professors Runge and Carathéodory and the Swiss student [Paul Finsler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Finsler "Paul Finsler"). Hilbert's assistant [Emmy Noether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Noether "Emmy Noether") and Käthe Heinemann were among the five women in attendance, and there were two blind students, Willi Windau and Friedrich Mittelsten Scheid.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20205-10) In winter 1916/17, there were seven attendees: Baade, [Richard Bär](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_B%C3%A4r "Richard Bär"), [Josef Engel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Engel "Josef Engel"), [Vsevolod Frederiks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vsevolod_Frederiks "Vsevolod Frederiks"), Heinemann, [Rudolf Jakob Humm](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rudolf_Jakob_Humm&action=edit&redlink=1 "Rudolf Jakob Humm (page does not exist)") ([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Jakob_Humm "de:Rudolf Jakob Humm")) and Windau.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20206-12) Klein sent a version of his summer 1917 lectures on general relativity to Albert Einstein, who dismissed the approach as overemphasising the formal over the heuristic point of view.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe20209-13) In 1927, the lectures were published as the second volume of _Vorlesungen über die Entwicklung der Mathematik im 19. Jahrhundert_, with the additional subtitle _Die Grundbegriffe der Invariantentheorie und ihr Eindringen in die mathematische Physik_ ('The Fundamental Concepts of Invariant Theory and Their Infiltration into Mathematical Physics'). The editors were Courant and especially [Stefan Cohn-Vossen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_Cohn-Vossen "Stefan Cohn-Vossen"),[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021539-14) who admitted the fragmentary character of the book in their introduction.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTECourantCohn-Vossen1979V-15)

The first volume is organised in eight chapters; the first chapter, simply titled "Gauß", is concerned with the life and work of [Carl Friedrich Gauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss "Carl Friedrich Gauss") and split into a section on applied and one on pure mathematics. The second chapter, "France and the École Polytechnique in the First Decades of the Nineteenth Century", contains sections on mechanics and mathematical physics (including the work of [Poisson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sim%C3%A9on_Denis_Poisson "Siméon Denis Poisson"), [Fourier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Fourier "Joseph Fourier") and [Cauchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustin-Louis_Cauchy "Augustin-Louis Cauchy")), geometry ([Monge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaspard_Monge "Gaspard Monge") and his followers), [analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_analysis "Mathematical analysis") and algebra (focusing on Cauchy and [Galois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89variste_Galois "Évariste Galois")). The third chapter "The Founding of Crelle's Journal and the Rise of Pure Mathematics in Germany" is concerned with mathematicians connected to _[Crelle's Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crelle%27s_Journal "Crelle's Journal")_ (the analysts [Dirichlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gustav_Lejeune_Dirichlet "Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet"), [Abel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niels_Henrik_Abel "Niels Henrik Abel") and [Jacobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Gustav_Jacob_Jacobi "Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi") and the geometers [Moebius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Ferdinand_M%C3%B6bius "August Ferdinand Möbius"), [Plücker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Pl%C3%BCcker "Julius Plücker") and [Steiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakob_Steiner "Jakob Steiner")), is followed by a chapter on "The Development of Algebraic Geometry after Moebius, Plücker and Steiner", with sections on [projective geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_geometry "Projective geometry"), invariant theory and _n_\-dimensional spaces and general complex numbers, including content on [Graßmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Grassmann "Hermann Grassmann") and [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Rowan_Hamilton "William Rowan Hamilton"). In the fifth chapter, "Mechanics and Mathematical Physics in Germany and England until about 1880", Klein discusses Hamilton's and Jacobi's works on mechanics and works of English mathematicians including [Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Green_/(mathematician/) "George Green (mathematician)"), [Stokes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_George_Stokes,_1st_Baronet "Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet") and [Maxwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell "James Clerk Maxwell"). Chapter 6, "The General Theory of Functions of Complex Variables according to Riemann and Weierstraß" contrasts [Riemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhard_Riemann "Bernhard Riemann")'s approach to [complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis "Complex analysis") with that of [Weierstraß](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Weierstrass "Karl Weierstrass"), and is followed by Chapter 7, "Deeper Insight into the Nature of Algebraic Varieties and Structures", which discusses algebraic geometry (including contributions by [Clebsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Clebsch "Alfred Clebsch") and [Noether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Noether "Emmy Noether")) and algebraic number theory ([Kummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Kummer "Ernst Kummer"), [Dedekind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Dedekind "Richard Dedekind") and [Hilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hilbert "David Hilbert"), among others). In the final chapter, "Group Theory and Function Theory; Automorphic Functions", Klein discusses first group theory in connection with the works of [Lagrange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph-Louis_Lagrange "Joseph-Louis Lagrange"), Galois and [C. Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Jordan "Camille Jordan"). In the section on automorphic forms, he treats hypergeometric functions, conformal mappings, the icosahedron and elliptic functions, including a few pages on [Poincaré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Poincar%C3%A9 "Henri Poincaré").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein1979Part_I,_pp._VII%E2%80%93XIII-16) Originally, Klein had also planned to include full chapters on Poincaré and [Sophus Lie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophus_Lie "Sophus Lie") in the book, but these are missing.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTECourantNeugebauer1979VI-9) Additionally, he planned to discuss [set theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_theory "Set theory"), the 1900 [International Congress of Mathematicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Congress_of_Mathematicians "International Congress of Mathematicians") and [Hilbert's problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_problems "Hilbert's problems").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021537%E2%80%93538-17)

The second volume is organised in three chapters. The first chapter, "Elementary Content regarding the Fundamentals of Linear Invariant Theory", is split into part A about general linear invariant theory and a "freer" part B about linear invariant theory including comments on the Erlangen Program and the development of vector and tensor analysis. The second chapter, "The Special Theory of Relativity in Mechanics and Mathematical Physics", has three parts: Part A is concerned with classical celestial mechanics, part B with Maxwell's electrodynamics and the [Lorentz group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_group "Lorentz group"), while part C treats the adaptation of mechanics to the relativity theory of the Lorentz group. The third chapter, "Transformation Groups on the Basis of a Quadratic Differential Form", has five parts. Part A treats [Lagrangian mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics "Lagrangian mechanics"), part B the intrinsic [differential geometry of surfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry_of_surfaces "Differential geometry of surfaces") following Gauß. The remaining parts are concerned with [Riemannian geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_geometry "Riemannian geometry"): part C contains the formal background of [Riemannian manifolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemannian_manifold "Riemannian manifold"), part D normal coordinates and geometric interpretations, and part E reports on the further development after the time of Riemann, including the work of [Beltrami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenio_Beltrami "Eugenio Beltrami"), [Lipschitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Lipschitz "Rudolf Lipschitz") and [Christoffel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elwin_Bruno_Christoffel "Elwin Bruno Christoffel").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein1979Part_II,_pp._VII%E2%80%93X-18) A planned fourth chapter on the general theory of relativity and Hamiltonian mechanics with a focus on contact transformations and Lie groups was not finished; the editors stated that none of the existing drafts could have been turned into a printable form without adding an additional author's thoughts to Klein's approach.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTECourantCohn-Vossen1979V-15) In contrast to the first volume, the second volume has a more systematic and factual focus and has fewer biographical and historical remarks.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFeigl1928-19)

Reception and legacy
--------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Reception and legacy")\]

The books were received enthusiastically and especially the first volume has been widely celebrated.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStrubecker1980-20)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTETobies2021537-5) [G. A. Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Abram_Miller "George Abram Miller"), reviewing the first volume in _[Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_/(journal/) "Science (journal)")_, sees Klein as the most eminent mathematician to write a general history and finds the "extremely difficult task ... well begun", and praises Klein's personal acquaintance with most leading mathematicians.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller1927-21) [Josef Lense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Lense "Josef Lense")'s review praises the editors and finds Klein the most suited person to the task.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTELense1928-22) [David Eugene Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Eugene_Smith "David Eugene Smith"), writing for the _[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulletin_of_the_American_Mathematical_Society "Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society")_, calls Klein a "master" and emphasises the lack of national prejudice in the work.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith1928-23) F. P. White's admiring review in _[The Mathematical Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mathematical_Gazette "The Mathematical Gazette")_ calls the book "fascinating" and mentions several "curious and entertaining" episodes.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite1927-24) The historian of mathematics [Heinrich Wieleitner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Wieleitner "Heinrich Wieleitner") reviewed both volumes for _[Isis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isis_/(journal/) "Isis (journal)")_. His review of the first volume warmly welcomes its publication and the information coming from Klein's personal involvement, but criticises some of Klein's methods as not up to the standards of scientific historiography. The overall verdict is that the book is _eine sehr wertvolle Vorarbeit zu einer wirklichen Geschichte der Mathematik des 19. Jahrh._ ('a very valuable preliminary work for a true history of 19th century mathematics').[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWieleitner1927-25) The second volume is described as incomplete but admirable. Although the reviewer notes a near-total lack of the personal touch of the first volume, he praises a few beautiful passages.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWieleitner1928-26)

The books had a great influence on [Dirk Jan Struik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirk_Jan_Struik "Dirk Jan Struik"), who had helped the editors in preparing the original manuscripts.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe2001591-27) In his later book _A Concise History of Mathematics_, Struik calls them "the best history of nineteenth century mathematics".[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStruik1967182-28) The Soviet mathematician [Vladimir Arnold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Arnold "Vladimir Arnold") deeply valued the books, and remarked in an interview that much of what he had learned about mathematics ("One-half of the mathematics I know", in his own words) came through their study.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTELui1997-29) He often recommended them to his students.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKhesinTabachnikov2012-30)

Reviewing the English edition of the book, the French mathematician [Jean Dieudonné](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dieudonn%C3%A9 "Jean Dieudonné") praises the idea of a new edition and notes that Klein's book has long been the only one on its topic, and still among the best. Nevertheless, he gives a long list of omissions and laments the lack of an index.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDieudonn%C3%A91981-31) In another French review of the German reprint of both volumes, Pierre Dugac calls the book "irreplaceable" and praises Klein's expressions of the "mood" of 19th century mathematics, but criticises the lack of a modern introduction putting the book in context of newer historical works.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDugac1982-32) Welcoming the reprint, the East German historian of mathematics [Hans Wußing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Wu%C3%9Fing "Hans Wußing") calls the book a part of the fundamental mathematical-historical literature, while noting that some of Klein's opinions are subjective and have been superseded.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWussing1980-33)

In his [book about Klein and Sophus Lie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein_and_Sophus_Lie "Felix Klein and Sophus Lie"), the Soviet mathematician [Isaak Yaglom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaak_Yaglom "Isaak Yaglom") defends Klein against accusations of chauvinism brought forward by [Jacques Hadamard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Hadamard "Jacques Hadamard") in 1943. While admitting that Klein ignored the contributions of Russian and Italian mathematicians and some fields like [probability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_theory "Probability theory"), Yaglom writes, "the book's import lies in the concept of joint work by scientists of all races and nationalities, contributing perhaps in different ways, but with equal merit, to the construction of the mathematical edifice."[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYaglom1988236-34) The mathematician and historian [Detlef Laugwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detlef_Laugwitz "Detlef Laugwitz") quotes Klein's _Vorlesungen_ in his book about [Bernhard Riemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhard_Riemann "Bernhard Riemann"), calling Klein "important as a witness of the effect of Riemann's ideas in the last decades of the 19th century".[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTELaugwitz1999150-35) The historian of mathematics [David E. Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_E._Rowe "David E. Rowe") describes them as "a highly personalized account of this period", and notes that the original lecture notes "were sometimes even more opinionated, expressing his misgivings about recent modernist trends toward [abstraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstraction_/(mathematics/) "Abstraction (mathematics)") and [axiomatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom "Axiom")".[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTERowe200493-36)

The book was translated into Russian twice, both times as Лекции о развитии математики в XIX столетии. The 1937 edition was translated by B. Livshits, [A. Lopshits](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Abram_Lopshits&action=edit&redlink=1 "Abram Lopshits (page does not exist)") ([ru](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%9B%D0%BE%D0%BF%D1%88%D0%B8%D1%86,_%D0%90%D0%B1%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%BC_%D0%9C%D0%B8%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%BD%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87 "ru:Лопшиц, Абрам Миронович")), [Y. Rabinovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Yuri_Rainich "George Yuri Rainich") and L. Tumerman and had a preface by the Soviet historian of mathematics [Mark Vygodskii](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mark_Vygodskii&action=edit&redlink=1 "Mark Vygodskii (page does not exist)") ([ru](https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/%D0%92%D1%8B%D0%B3%D0%BE%D0%B4%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9,_%D0%9C%D0%B0%D1%80%D0%BA_%D0%AF%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%B2%D0%B8%D1%87 "ru:Выгодский, Марк Яковлевич"); [de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Jakowlewitsch_Wygodski "de:Mark Jakowlewitsch Wygodski")).[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein1937-37) It contained some errors. For example, it mistranslated Jacobi dying from _Blattern_ (smallpox) as dying in a place called Blattern.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYaglom1988210-38) The second version appeared in 1989, translated by N. M. Nagorny and edited by [M. M. Postnikov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Postnikov "Mikhail Postnikov").[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKerimov2008-39) In the preface, which builds on Vygodskii's, they noted that their main focus was to be as faithful as possible to Klein's thought and the spirit of his work.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein19893,_7-40) In 2003, also the second volume appeared, translated by [V. A. Antonov](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vadim_Anatol%27evich_Antonov&action=edit&redlink=1 "Vadim Anatol'evich Antonov (page does not exist)") and edited by B. P. Kondratyev.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein2003-41)

The book was translated into English by M. Ackerman as _Development of Mathematics in The 19th Century_ (1979), edited by [Robert Hermann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hermann_/(mathematician/) "Robert Hermann (mathematician)"), who provided a lengthy appendix on "Kleinian Mathematics from an Advanced Standpoint".[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein1979a-42) It was translated into Chinese as 数学在19世纪的发展 as part of the 数学翻译丛书 (Mathematical Translations series) edited by [Shing-Tung Yau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shing-Tung_Yau "Shing-Tung Yau") for [Higher Education Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_Education_Press "Higher Education Press"). The first volume appeared in 2010, translated by [Qi Minyou](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Qi_Minyou&action=edit&redlink=1 "Qi Minyou (page does not exist)") ([zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%BD%90%E6%B0%91%E5%8F%8B "zh:齐民友")); the second in 2011, translated by Li Peilian (李培廉). The first volume includes a translation into Chinese of Hermann's preface to the English translation.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein2010-43)[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorlesungen_%C3%BCber_die_Entwicklung_der_Mathematik_im_19._Jahrhundert#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein2011-44)

Abstract
--------

Forty-five participants representing 12 countries took part in the symposium, which featured 29 lectures covering a variety of topics from the era of Euler and Clairaut to the onset of modern electronic computers. The principal theme of the meeting, discussed in about half of the papers presented, concerned issues and ideas at the interface between pure and applied mathematics. This theme arose in several historical contexts ranging from early 19th-century France to Wilhelmian Germany and beyond to the United States during the Second World War. Other topics that received considerable attention included the emergence of projective geometry and the influence of projective concepts of geometry in general, Abel's theorem and its role in algebraic geometry, the geometric background of transformation group theory, contrasting notions of rigor in 18th-and 19th-century mathematics, the philosophical views of Cantor and Kronecker and subsequent developments in the foundations of mathematics, 19th-century American algebra, and number theory from Gauss to Hilbert. The following abstracts of these lectures are given in the order in which they were presented: CORE Metadata, citation and similar papers at core.ac.uk

Key takeaways

![Image 7: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)AI




-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.  The symposium featured 29 lectures from 45 participants across 12 countries, addressing modern mathematics' historical evolution.
2.  Half of the discussions focused on the intersection of pure and applied mathematics through various historical contexts.
3.  Key topics included projective geometry, Abel's theorem in algebraic geometry, and contrasting rigor in 18th-19th century mathematics.
4.  Notable figures discussed include Lagrange, Liouville, Cantor, and Klein, highlighting their contributions to mathematical foundations.
5.  The text emphasizes the evolving views on applied mathematics in German academia during the late 19th century.

This paper traces the ebbs and flows of the history of geometry at Cambridge from the time of Cayley to 1940, and therefore the arrival of a branch of modern mathematics in Great Britain. [Maria D. Chalkou, State High School Advisor, PhD with "Summa cum Laude" (NKUA), MSc mathematician, editor of Codex Vindobonensis phil. Gr. 65, 15th cent. ff.(11r-126r)-2006, and Codex 72 of the Library of Dimitsana, 18th cent.-2009](https://en-uoa-gr.academia.edu/DrChalkou)

The paper concerns topics of arithmetic, algebra and geometry which are included in the publication of the Codex Vindobonensis phil. Gr. 65 ff. (11r-126r) of the 15th c. (Chalkou, 2006), and of the manuscript 72 of the 18th c. of the historical Library of Demetsana (Chalkou, 2009). During the study of the 2 manuscripts the interest mainly focused on the mathematical analysis of the methods of the authors, and their significance in the development of the History of Mathematics. The paper also aims to highlight the necessity of easier and broader access to the Sources of Cultural Heritage and the value of digitizing its archives. We attempt to briefly describe the time the 2 codes were written, the language, the influences and the mathematical fields which comprise their content. We make known the findings which consolidated the view that the Byzantine manuscripts the Mathematical Encyclopedia of the Byzantines, while the manuscript 72 of the 18th c. is one of the first texts with non-elementary Mathematics during Ottoman rule, and it includes Euclidean Geometry by Nikephoros Theotokes, topics of algebra but also the commercial Mathematics of the Byzantines. From the ‘Mathemataria’ which were found in the School of Demetsana it is evident that the students were taught, among other things, theoretical and practical arithmetic as well as Euclidean geometry from the manuscript 72, which covered syllabus of today’s junior and senior high school. The School was considered higher, and certain manuscripts which were found in its library contain material which is basic but of university level. The anonymous author of Codex 65 writes that his main source is the work of Greek scholars, and that he has been influenced by the Hindus, the Chinese and the Persians through the Latin scholars due to the commercial transactions between the Byzantines and the West. In the Codex 65we discovered categories of problems whose solution is achieved through methods unknown to this day. During the research we studied reliable sources of the History of Mathematics in which no data related to these methods were found (Loria and Kovaios, 1972) and (Heath, 1921) and (Smith, 1958). Then certain methods led us to formulate and prove new mathematical propositions in the field of number theory.

What differences characterized the approach of Lagrange and Lazare Carnot to mathematics?add

The paper indicates that Lagrange epitomized a general theoretical approach, whereas Carnot exemplified engineering-focused applications. Their contrasting methodologies reflect broader debates within early 19th century French mathematics.

How did Joseph Liouville's work influence differential geometry and classical mechanics?add

Liouville's interpretation of the principle of least action contributed significantly to the Hamilton-Jacobi equations, bridging differential geometry and classical mechanics. He was able to treat particle motion as geodesic motion on a surface, enhancing understanding well before Riemann's contributions.

What led to the establishment of the Berlin Technische Hochschule in 1879?add

The Berlin Technische Hochschule emerged from the merger of the Berlin Bauakademie and Gewerbeakademie, enhancing its academic status. The 1916 incorporation of the Bergakademie further enriched its mathematical programs with notable educators.

How did Felix Klein attempt to reconcile pure and applied mathematics in 19th-century Germany?add

Klein sought to balance the increasing specialization in mathematical research with its applications, particularly at educational institutions. His efforts aimed to integrate pure and applied mathematics, particularly within the context of competing institutional frameworks.

What role did mathematical societies play in the promotion of applied mathematics in Germany?add

The Deutsche Mathematiker-Vereinigung, established in 1890, sought to combat perceptions of applied mathematics as inferior. By improving teacher training to focus on practical applications, organizations influenced a shift towards valuing applied mathematics.

> Everyone knows what a curve is, until he has studied enough mathematics to become confused through the countless number of possible exceptions.

Christian Felix Klein was a German mathematician and mathematics educator, known for his work with group theory, complex analysis, non-Euclidean geometry, and on the associations between geometry and group theory. His 1872 Erlangen program, classifying geometries by their basic symmetry groups, was an influential synthesis of much of the mathematics of the time.

Life
----

Felix Klein was born on 25 April 1849 in Düsseldorf, to Prussian parents; his father, Caspar Klein 1809–1889, was a Prussian government official's secretary stationed in the Rhine Province. Klein's mother was Sophie Elise Klein 1819–1890, née Kayser. He attended the Gymnasium in Düsseldorf, then studied mathematics and physics at the University of Bonn, 1865–1866, intending to become a physicist. At that time, Julius Plücker had Bonn's professorship of mathematics and experimental physics, but by the time Klein became his assistant, during 1866, Plücker's interest was geometry. Klein received his doctorate, supervised by Plücker, from the University of Bonn during 1868.

Plücker died during 1868, leaving his book concerning the basis of line geometry incomplete. Klein was the obvious person to complete the second part of Plücker's Neue Geometrie des Raumes, and thus became acquainted with Alfred Clebsch, who had relocated to Göttingen during 1868. Klein visited Clebsch the next year, along with visits to Berlin and Paris. During July 1870, at the beginning of the Franco-Prussian War, he was in Paris and had to leave the country. For a brief time he served as a medical orderly in the Prussian army before being appointed lecturer at Göttingen during early 1871.

Erlangen appointed Klein professor during 1872, when he was only 23 years old. For this, he was endorsed by Clebsch, who regarded him as likely to become the best mathematician of his time. Klein did not desire a school at Erlangen where there were few students, and so he was pleased to be offered a professorship at Munich's Technische Hochschule during 1875. There he and Alexander von Brill taught advanced courses to many excellent students, including, Adolf Hurwitz, Walther von Dyck, Karl Rohn, Carl Runge, Max Planck, Luigi Bianchi, and Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro.

During 1875 Klein married Anne Hegel, the granddaughter of the philosopher Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel.

After five years at the Technische Hochschule, Klein was appointed to a chair of geometry at Leipzig. There his colleagues included Walther von Dyck, Rohn, Eduard Study and Friedrich Engel. Klein's years at Leipzig, 1880 to 1886, fundamentally changed his life. During 1882, his health collapsed; during 1883–1884, he was plagued by depression. Nonetheless his research continued; his seminal work on hyperelliptic sigma functions dates from around this period, being published during 1886 and 1888.

Klein accepted a professorship at the University of Göttingen during 1886. From then until his 1913 retirement, he sought to re-establish Göttingen as the world's main mathematics research center. Yet he never managed to transfer from Leipzig to Göttingen his own primacy as a developer of geometry. At Göttingen, he taught a variety of courses, mainly concerning the interface between mathematics and physics, such as mechanics and potential theory.

The research facility Klein established at Göttingen served as a model for the best such facilities throughout the world. He introduced weekly discussion meetings, and created a mathematical reading room and library. During 1895, Klein hired David Hilbert away from the University of Königsberg; this appointment proved fateful, because Hilbert continued Göttingen's good reputation until his own retirement during 1932.

With Klein's editorship, Mathematische Annalen became one of the best mathematics journals in the world. Founded by Clebsch, only with Klein's management did it first rival then surpass Crelle's Journal based in the University of Berlin. Klein established a small team of editors who met regularly, making democratic decisions. The journal specialized in complex analysis, algebraic geometry, and invariant theory at least until Hilbert ended the subject. It also provided an important outlet for real analysis and the new group theory.

![Image 16](https://geniuses.club/public/storage/136/198/019/039/500_0_606ee473eb24c.png)

Klein during his Leipzig period.

During 1893 in Chicago, Klein was a major speaker at the International Mathematical Congress held as part of the World's Columbian Exposition. Due partly to Klein's efforts, Göttingen began admitting women during 1893. He supervised the first Ph.D. thesis in mathematics written at Göttingen by a woman; she was Grace Chisholm Young, an English student of Arthur Cayley's, whom Klein admired. During 1897 Klein became a foreign member of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences.

About 1900, Klein began to become interested in mathematical instruction in schools. During 1905, he was decisive in formulating a plan recommending that analytic geometry, the rudiments of differential and integral calculus, and the function concept be taught in secondary schools. This recommendation was gradually implemented in many countries around the world. During 1908, Klein was elected president of the International Commission on Mathematical Instruction at the Rome International Congress of Mathematicians. With his guidance, the German part of the Commission published many volumes on the teaching of mathematics at all levels in Germany.

The London Mathematical Society awarded Klein its De Morgan Medal during 1893. He was elected a member of the Royal Society during 1885, and was awarded its Copley Medal during 1912. He retired the next year due to ill health, but continued to teach mathematics at his home for some years more.

Klein was one of the 93 signatories of the Manifesto of the Ninety-Three, a document penned in support of the German invasion of Belgium in the early stages of World War I.

Klein had the title of Geheimrat trusted-advisor.

He died in Göttingen during 1925.

Work
----

Klein's dissertation, on line geometry and its applications to mechanics, classified second degree line complexes using Weierstrass's theory of elementary divisors.

Klein's first important mathematical discoveries were made during 1870. In collaboration with Sophus Lie, he discovered the fundamental properties of the asymptotic lines on the Kummer surface. They later investigated W-curves, curves invariant under a group of projective transformations. It was Lie who introduced Klein to the concept of group, which was to have a major role in his later work. Klein also learned about groups from Camille Jordan.

Klein devised the "Klein bottle" named after him, a one-sided closed surface which cannot be embedded in three-dimensional Euclidean space, but it may be immersed as a cylinder looped back through itself to join with its other end from the "inside". It may be embedded in the Euclidean space of dimensions 4 and higher. The concept of a Klein Bottle was devised as a 3-Dimensional Möbius strip, with one method of construction being the attachment of the edges of two Möbius strips.

During the 1890s, Klein began studying mathematical physics more intensively, writing on the gyroscope with Arnold Sommerfeld. During 1894, he initiated the idea of an encyclopedia of mathematics including its applications, which became the Encyklopädie der mathematischen Wissenschaften. This enterprise, which endured until 1935, provided an important standard reference of enduring value.

### Erlangen program

During 1871, while at Göttingen, Klein made major discoveries in geometry. He published two papers On the So-called Non-Euclidean Geometry showing that Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometries could be considered metric spaces determined by a Cayley-Klein metric. This insight had the corollary that non-Euclidean geometry was consistent if and only if Euclidean geometry was, giving the same status to geometries Euclidean and non-Euclidean, and ending all controversy about non-Euclidean geometry. Arthur Cayley never accepted Klein's argument, believing it to be circular.

Klein's synthesis of geometry as the study of the properties of a space that is invariant under a given group of transformations, known as the Erlangen program 1872, profoundly influenced the evolution of mathematics. This program was initiated by Klein's inaugural lecture as professor at Erlangen, although it was not the actual speech he gave on the occasion. The program proposed a unified system of geometry that has become the accepted modern method. Klein showed how the essential properties of a given geometry could be represented by the group of transformations that preserve those properties. Thus the program's definition of geometry encompassed both Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometry.

Presently the significance of Klein's contributions to geometry is more than evident, but not because those contributions are now considered strange or wrong. On the contrary, those contributions have become so much a part of our present mathematical thinking that it is difficult for us to appreciate their novelty, and the way in which they were not immediately accepted by all his contemporaries.

### Complex analysis

Klein saw his work on complex analysis as his major contribution to mathematics, specifically his work on:

*   The link between certain ideas of Riemann's and invariant theory,
*   Number theory and abstract algebra;
*   Group theory;
*   Geometry with more than 3 dimensions and differential equations, especially equations he invented, namely elliptic modular functions and automorphic functions.

Klein showed that the modular group moves the fundamental region of the complex plane so as to tessellate that plane. During 1879, he examined the action of PSL2,7, considered as an image of the modular group, and obtained an explicit representation of a Riemann surface now termed the Klein quartic. He showed that that surface was a curve in projective space, that its equation was x3y + y3z + z3x = 0, and that its group of symmetries was PSL2,7 of order 168. His Ueber Riemann's Theorie der algebraischen Funktionen und ihre Integrale 1882 treats complex analysis in a geometric way, connecting potential theory and conformal mappings. This work drew on notions from fluid dynamics.

Klein considered equations of degree > 4, and was especially interested in using transcendental methods to solve the general equation of the fifth degree. Building on the methods of Charles Hermite and Leopold Kronecker, he produced similar results to those of Brioschi and later completely solved the problem by means of the icosahedral group. This work enabled him to write a series of papers on elliptic modular functions.

In his 1884 book on the icosahedron, Klein established a theory of automorphic functions, associating algebra and geometry. However Poincaré published an outline of his theory of automorphic functions during 1881, which resulted in a friendly rivalry between the two men. Both sought to state and prove a grand uniformization theorem that would establish the new theory more completely. Klein succeeded in formulating such a theorem and in describing a strategy for proving it. But while doing this work his health decreased, as mentioned above.

Klein summarized his work on automorphic and elliptic modular functions in a four volume treatise, written with Robert Fricke during a period of about 20 years.

**Felix Christian Klein** (;[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-1) German: [\[klaɪn\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German"); 25 April 1849 – 22 June 1925) was a German [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematician "Mathematician"), [mathematics educator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics_education "Mathematics education") and [historian of mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_mathematics "History of mathematics"), known for his work in [group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory "Group theory"), [complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis "Complex analysis"), [non-Euclidean geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Euclidean_geometry "Non-Euclidean geometry"), and the associations between [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry "Geometry") and [group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory "Group theory"). His 1872 [Erlangen program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erlangen_program "Erlangen program") classified geometries by their basic [symmetry groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_group "Symmetry group") and was an influential synthesis of much of the mathematics of the time.

During his tenure at the [University of Göttingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_G%C3%B6ttingen "University of Göttingen"), Klein was able to turn it into a center for mathematical and scientific research through the establishment of new lectures, professorships, and institutes. His [seminars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein_Protocols "Felix Klein Protocols") covered most areas of mathematics then known as well as their applications. Klein also devoted considerable time to mathematical instruction and promoted mathematics education reform at all grade levels in Germany and abroad. He became the first president of the [International Commission on Mathematical Instruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Commission_on_Mathematical_Instruction "International Commission on Mathematical Instruction") in 1908 at the Fourth International Congress of Mathematicians in Rome.

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Felix_Klein%2C_Leipzig_years.png/250px-Felix_Klein%2C_Leipzig_years.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Felix_Klein,_Leipzig_years.png)

Klein during his Leipzig period.

Felix Klein was born on 25 April 1849 in [Düsseldorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCsseldorf "Düsseldorf"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-2) to [Prussian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussia "Prussia") parents. His father, Caspar Klein (1809–1889), was a Prussian government official's secretary stationed in the [Rhine Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhine_Province "Rhine Province"). His mother was Sophie Elise Klein (1819–1890, [née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Name_at_birth "Name at birth") Kayser).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-3) He attended the [Gymnasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnasium_/(school/) "Gymnasium (school)") in Düsseldorf, then studied mathematics and physics at the [University of Bonn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bonn "University of Bonn"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-4) 1865–1866, intending to become a physicist. At that time, [Julius Plücker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Pl%C3%BCcker "Julius Plücker") had Bonn's professorship of mathematics and experimental physics, but by the time Klein became his assistant, in 1866, Plücker's interest was mainly geometry. Klein received his doctorate, supervised by Plücker, from the University of Bonn in 1868.

Plücker died in 1868, leaving his book concerning the basis of [line geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_geometry "Line geometry") incomplete. Klein was the obvious person to complete the second part of Plücker's _Neue Geometrie des Raumes_, and thus became acquainted with [Alfred Clebsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Clebsch "Alfred Clebsch"), who had relocated to Göttingen in 1868. Klein visited Clebsch the next year, along with visits to [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and Paris. In July 1870, at the beginning of the [Franco-Prussian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War "Franco-Prussian War"), he was in Paris and had to leave the country. For a brief time he served as a medical orderly in the [Prussian army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussian_army "Prussian army") before being appointed _Privatdozent_ (lecturer) at Göttingen in early 1871.

The [University of Erlangen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Erlangen%E2%80%93Nuremberg "University of Erlangen–Nuremberg") appointed Klein professor in 1872, when he was only 23 years old.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-5) For this, he was endorsed by Clebsch, who regarded him as likely to become the best mathematician of his time. Klein did not wish to remain in Erlangen, where there were very few students, and was pleased to be offered a professorship at the [Technische Hochschule München](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_University_of_Munich "Technical University of Munich") in 1875. There he and [Alexander von Brill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Brill "Alexander von Brill") taught advanced courses to many excellent students, including [Adolf Hurwitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hurwitz "Adolf Hurwitz"), [Walther von Dyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_von_Dyck "Walther von Dyck"), [Karl Rohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Rohn "Karl Rohn"), [Carl Runge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Runge "Carl Runge"), [Max Planck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Planck "Max Planck"), [Luigi Bianchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Bianchi "Luigi Bianchi"), and [Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorio_Ricci-Curbastro "Gregorio Ricci-Curbastro").

In 1875, Klein married Anne Hegel, granddaughter of the philosopher [Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Wilhelm_Friedrich_Hegel "Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-6)

After spending five years at the Technische Hochschule, Klein was appointed to a chair of [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry "Geometry") at [Leipzig University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig_University "Leipzig University"). His colleagues included [Walther von Dyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_von_Dyck "Walther von Dyck"), Rohn, [Eduard Study](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eduard_Study "Eduard Study") and [Friedrich Engel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Engel_/(mathematician/) "Friedrich Engel (mathematician)"). Klein's years at Leipzig, 1880 to 1886, fundamentally changed his life. In 1882, his health collapsed and he battled with depression for the next two years.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-7) Nevertheless, his research continued; his seminal work on hyperelliptic sigma functions, published between 1886 and 1888, dates from around this period.

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Max_Liebermann_Felix_Klein_1912.png/250px-Max_Liebermann_Felix_Klein_1912.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Max_Liebermann_Felix_Klein_1912.png)

Klein (1912). Painting of [Max Liebermann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Liebermann "Max Liebermann").

Klein accepted a professorship at the [University of Göttingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_G%C3%B6ttingen "University of Göttingen") in 1886. From then on, until his 1913 retirement, he sought to re-establish Göttingen as the world's prime center for mathematics research. However, he never managed to transfer from Leipzig to Göttingen his own leading role as developer of [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry "Geometry"). He taught a variety of courses at Göttingen, mainly concerning the interface between mathematics and physics, in particular, [mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanics "Mechanics") and [potential theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_theory "Potential theory").

The research facility Klein established at Göttingen served as model for the best such facilities throughout the world. He introduced weekly discussion meetings, and created a mathematical reading room and library. In 1895, Klein recruited [David Hilbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hilbert "David Hilbert") from the [University of Königsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_K%C3%B6nigsberg "University of Königsberg"). This appointment proved of great importance; Hilbert continued to enhance Göttingen's primacy in mathematics until his own retirement in 1932. Klein and Hilbert jointly invited [Emmy Noether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Noether "Emmy Noether") to Göttingen in 1915 where she introduced Einstein to group theory and the relationship between symmetries and conservation principles.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-8)

Under Klein's editorship, _[Mathematische Annalen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematische_Annalen "Mathematische Annalen")_ became one of the best mathematical journals in the world. Founded by Clebsch, it grew under Klein's management, to rival, and eventually surpass _[Crelle's Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crelle%27s_Journal "Crelle's Journal")_, based at the [University of Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Berlin "University of Berlin"). Klein established a small team of editors who met regularly, making decisions in a democratic spirit. The journal first specialized in [complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis "Complex analysis"), [algebraic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_geometry "Algebraic geometry"), and [invariant theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_theory "Invariant theory"). It also provided an important outlet for [real analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_analysis "Real analysis") and the new [group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory "Group theory").

In 1893, Klein was a major speaker at the International Mathematical Congress held in Chicago as part of the [World's Columbian Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World%27s_Columbian_Exposition "World's Columbian Exposition").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-9) Due partly to Klein's efforts, Göttingen began admitting women in 1893. He supervised the first Ph.D. thesis in mathematics written at Göttingen by a woman, by [Grace Chisholm Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Chisholm_Young "Grace Chisholm Young"), an English student of [Arthur Cayley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Cayley "Arthur Cayley")'s, whom Klein admired. In 1897, Klein became a foreign member of the [Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Netherlands_Academy_of_Arts_and_Sciences "Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-10)

Around 1900, Klein began to become interested in mathematical instruction in schools. In 1905, he was instrumental in formulating a plan recommending that [analytic geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_geometry "Analytic geometry"), the rudiments of differential and integral [calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus "Calculus"), and the [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_/(mathematics/) "Function (mathematics)") concept be taught in secondary schools.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-12) This recommendation was gradually implemented in many countries around the world. In 1908, Klein was elected president of the [International Commission on Mathematical Instruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Commission_on_Mathematical_Instruction "International Commission on Mathematical Instruction") at the Rome [International Congress of Mathematicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Congress_of_Mathematicians "International Congress of Mathematicians").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-13) Under his guidance, the German part of the Commission published many volumes on the teaching of mathematics at all levels in Germany. In 1892 the [Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Literary_and_Philosophical_Society "Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society") awarded Klein Honorary membership of the Society.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-14) The [London Mathematical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Mathematical_Society "London Mathematical Society") awarded Klein its [De Morgan Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Morgan_Medal "De Morgan Medal") in 1893. He was elected a member of the [Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society "Royal Society") in 1885, and was awarded its [Copley Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copley_Medal "Copley Medal") in 1912. He retired the following year due to ill health, but continued to teach mathematics at his home for several further years.

Klein was one of ninety-three signatories of the [Manifesto of the Ninety-Three](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifesto_of_the_Ninety-Three "Manifesto of the Ninety-Three"), a document penned in support of the German invasion of Belgium in the early stages of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I").

He died in Göttingen in 1925.

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/87/Mobius_to_Klein.gif)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mobius_to_Klein.gif)

Construction of a Klein Bottle from two Möbius strips

Klein's dissertation, on [line geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_geometry "Line geometry") and its applications to [mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanics "Mechanics"), classified second degree line complexes using [Weierstrass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weierstrass "Weierstrass")'s theory of elementary divisors.

Klein's first important mathematical discoveries were made in 1870. In collaboration with [Sophus Lie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophus_Lie "Sophus Lie"), he discovered the fundamental properties of the asymptotic lines on the [Kummer surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kummer_surface "Kummer surface"). They later investigated [W-curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W-curve "W-curve"), curves invariant under a group of [projective transformations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_transformation "Projective transformation"). It was Lie who introduced Klein to the concept of group, which was to have a major role in his later work. Klein also learned about groups from [Camille Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Jordan "Camille Jordan").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-15)

Klein devised the "[Klein bottle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klein_bottle "Klein bottle")" named after him, a one-sided closed surface which cannot be embedded in three-dimensional [Euclidean space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_space "Euclidean space"), but it may be immersed as a cylinder looped back through itself to join with its other end from the "inside". It may be embedded in the Euclidean space of dimensions 4 and higher. The concept of a Klein Bottle was devised as a 3-Dimensional [Möbius strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius_strip "Möbius strip"), with one method of construction being the attachment of the edges of two [Möbius strips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius_strip "Möbius strip").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-16)

During the 1890s, Klein began studying [mathematical physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_physics "Mathematical physics") more intensively, writing on the [gyroscope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyroscope "Gyroscope") with [Arnold Sommerfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Sommerfeld "Arnold Sommerfeld").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-17) During 1894, he initiated the idea of an encyclopedia of mathematics including its applications, which became the [_Encyklopädie der mathematischen Wissenschaften_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klein%27s_Encyclopedia_of_Mathematical_Sciences "Klein's Encyclopedia of Mathematical Sciences"). This enterprise, which endured until 1935, provided an important standard reference of enduring value.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-18)

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Non-euclidean-geometry-model.svg/330px-Non-euclidean-geometry-model.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Non-euclidean-geometry-model.svg)

Non-Euclidean geometry models proposed by Klein (left) and Poincaré (right)

In 1871, while at Göttingen, Klein made major discoveries in geometry. He published two papers _On the So-called Non-Euclidean Geometry_ showing that Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometries could be considered [metric spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_space "Metric space") determined by a [Cayley–Klein metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayley%E2%80%93Klein_metric "Cayley–Klein metric"). This insight had the corollary that [non-Euclidean geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Euclidean_geometry "Non-Euclidean geometry") was consistent if and only if [Euclidean geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_geometry "Euclidean geometry") was, giving the same status to geometries Euclidean and non-Euclidean, and ending all controversy about non-Euclidean geometry. [Arthur Cayley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Cayley "Arthur Cayley") never accepted Klein's argument, believing it to be circular.

Klein's synthesis of [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry "Geometry") as the study of the properties of a space that is invariant under a given [group of transformations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformation_group "Transformation group"), known as the _[Erlangen program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erlangen_program "Erlangen program")_ (1872), profoundly influenced the evolution of mathematics. This program was initiated by Klein's inaugural lecture as professor at Erlangen, although it was not the actual speech he gave on the occasion. The program proposed a unified system of geometry that has become the accepted modern method. Klein showed how the essential properties of a given geometry could be represented by the group of [transformations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformation_group "Transformation group") that preserve those properties. Thus the program's definition of geometry encompassed both Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometry.

Currently, the significance of Klein's contributions to geometry is evident. They have become so much part of mathematical thinking that it is difficult to appreciate their novelty when first presented, and understand the fact that they were not immediately accepted by all his contemporaries.

Klein saw his work on [complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis "Complex analysis") as his major contribution to mathematics, specifically his work on:

*   The link between certain ideas of [Riemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernhard_Riemann "Bernhard Riemann") and [invariant theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_theory "Invariant theory"),
*   [Number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory "Number theory") and [abstract algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_algebra "Abstract algebra");
*   [Group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory "Group theory");
*   [Geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry "Geometry") in more than 3 dimensions and [differential equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_equations "Differential equations"), especially equations he invented, satisfied by [elliptic modular functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_modular_function "Elliptic modular function") and [automorphic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphic_function "Automorphic function").

Klein showed that the [modular group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_group "Modular group") moves the fundamental region of the [complex plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_plane "Complex plane") so as to [tessellate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessellation "Tessellation") the plane. In 1879, he examined the action of [PSL(2,7)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PSL/(2,7/) "PSL(2,7)"), considered as an image of the [modular group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_group "Modular group"), and obtained an explicit representation of a [Riemann surface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_surface "Riemann surface") now termed the [Klein quartic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klein_quartic "Klein quartic"). He showed that it was a complex curve in [projective space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projective_space "Projective space"), that its equation was _x_3_y_ + _y_3_z_ + _z_3_x_ = 0, and that its group of [symmetries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_group "Symmetry group") was [PSL(2,7)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PSL/(2,7/) "PSL(2,7)") of [order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_/(group_theory/) "Order (group theory)") 168. His _Ueber Riemann's Theorie der algebraischen Funktionen und ihre Integrale_ (1882) treats complex analysis in a geometric way, connecting [potential theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_theory "Potential theory") and [conformal mappings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_mapping "Conformal mapping"). This work drew on notions from [fluid dynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid_dynamics "Fluid dynamics").

Klein considered equations of degree > 4, and was especially interested in using transcendental methods to solve the general equation of the fifth degree. Building on methods of [Charles Hermite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Hermite "Charles Hermite") and [Leopold Kronecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopold_Kronecker "Leopold Kronecker"), he produced similar results to those of Brioschi and later completely solved the problem by means of the [icosahedral group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icosahedral_group "Icosahedral group"). This work enabled him to write a series of papers on [elliptic modular functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_modular_function "Elliptic modular function").

In his 1884 book on the [icosahedron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icosahedron "Icosahedron"), Klein established a theory of [automorphic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphic_function "Automorphic function"), associating algebra and geometry. [Poincaré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Poincar%C3%A9 "Henri Poincaré") had published an outline of his theory of automorphic functions in 1881, which resulted in a friendly rivalry between the two men. Both sought to state and prove a grand [uniformization theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniformization_theorem "Uniformization theorem") that would establish the new theory more completely. Klein succeeded in formulating such a theorem and in describing a strategy for proving it. He came up with his proof during an [asthma attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asthma_attack "Asthma attack") at 2:30 A.M. on 23 March 1882.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Klein#cite_note-19)

Klein summarized his work on [automorphic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automorphic_function "Automorphic function") and [elliptic modular functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_modular_function "Elliptic modular function") in a four volume treatise, written with [Robert Fricke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fricke "Robert Fricke") over a period of about 20 years.

,  Mikhail G. Katz M. Katz, Department of Mathematics, Bar Ilan University, Ramat Gan 5290002 Israel [katzmik@math.biu.ac.il](mailto:katzmik@math.biu.ac.il) ,  Karl Kuhlemann K. Kuhlemann, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz University Hannover, D-30167 Hannover, Germany [kus.kuhlemann@t-online.de](mailto:kus.kuhlemann@t-online.de) ,  Jan Peter Schäfermeyer J. P. Schäfermeyer, Berlin, Germany [jpschaefermeyer@gmail.com](mailto:jpschaefermeyer@gmail.com)  and  David Sherry D. Sherry, Department of Philosophy, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ 86011, US [David.Sherry@nau.edu](mailto:David.Sherry@nau.edu)

###### Abstract.

An alleged opposition between David Hilbert and Felix Klein as modern _vs_ countermodern has been pursued by marxist historian Herbert Mehrtens and others. Scholars such as Epple, Grattan-Guinness, Gray, Quinn, Rowe, and recently Siegmund-Schultze and Mazzotti have voiced a range of opinions concerning Mehrtens’ dialectical methodology. We explore contrasting perspectives on Klein’s contested modernism, as well as Hilbert’s and Klein’s views on intuition, logic, and physics. We analyze Jeremy Gray’s comment on Klein’s ethnographic speculations concerning Jewish mathematicians and find it to be untenable. We argue that Mehrtens was looking for countermoderns at the wrong address.

###### Key words and phrases:

Arithmetized analysis; intuition; logic; physics; moderns; countermoderns; antisemitism; David Hilbert; Felix Klein

###### 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification:

01A60; 01A61

###### Contents

    2.  [7.2 Physics as seen by Hilbert and Klein](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.00122v1#S7.SS2 "7.2. Physics as seen by Hilbert and Klein ‣ 7. Geometry, intuition, logic, physics ‣ Exploring Felix Klein’s contested modernism")
    3.  [7.3 Differences according to Max Born](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.00122v1#S7.SS3 "7.3. Differences according to Max Born ‣ 7. Geometry, intuition, logic, physics ‣ Exploring Felix Klein’s contested modernism")
    4.  [7.4 Hilbert’s formalism](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.00122v1#S7.SS4 "7.4. Hilbert’s formalism ‣ 7. Geometry, intuition, logic, physics ‣ Exploring Felix Klein’s contested modernism")
