[![Image 21](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F%2C_003.jpg/250px-Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F%2C_003.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F,_003.jpg)

A student draws his professor of mathematics: Gauss sketched by his student [Johann Benedict Listing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Benedict_Listing "Johann Benedict Listing"), 1830

In the first two decades of the 19th century, Gauss was the only important mathematician in Germany comparable to the leading French mathematicians.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Schubring-86) His _Disquisitiones Arithmeticae_ was the first mathematical book from Germany to be translated into the French language.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-87)

Gauss was "in front of the new development" with documented research since 1799, his wealth of new ideas, and his rigour of demonstration.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein1894100%E2%80%93101-88) In contrast to previous mathematicians like [Leonhard Euler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonhard_Euler "Leonhard Euler"), who let their readers take part in their reasoning, including certain erroneous deviations from the correct path,[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein19795%E2%80%936-89) Gauss introduced a new style of direct and complete exposition that did not attempt to show the reader the author's train of thought.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington2004217-90)

> Gauss was the first to restore that _rigor_ of demonstration which we admire in the ancients and which had been forced unduly into the background by the exclusive interest of the preceding period in _new_ developments.

— [Klein 1894](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#CITEREFKlein1894), p. 101

But for himself, he propagated a quite different ideal, given in a letter to Farkas Bolyai as follows:[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-91)

> It is not knowledge, but the act of learning, not possession but the act of getting there, which grants the greatest enjoyment. When I have clarified and exhausted a subject, then I turn away from it, in order to go into darkness again.

— [Dunnington 2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#CITEREFDunnington2004), p. 416

His posthumous papers, his scientific [diary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_diary "Gauss's diary"),[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-92) and short glosses in his own textbooks show that he empirically worked to a great extent.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann19224%E2%80%936-93)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger193318-94) He was a lifelong busy and enthusiastic calculator, working extraordinarily quickly and checking his results through estimation. Nevertheless, his calculations were not always free from mistakes.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaennchen193064%E2%80%9365-95) He coped with the enormous workload by using skillful tools.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaennchen19304%E2%80%939-96) Gauss used numerous [mathematical tables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_table "Mathematical table"), examined their exactness, and constructed new tables on various matters for personal use.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-97) He developed new tools for effective calculation, for example the [Gaussian elimination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_elimination "Gaussian elimination").[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-98) Gauss's calculations and the tables he prepared were often more precise than practically necessary.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaennchen19303-99) Very likely, this method gave him additional material for his theoretical work.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaennchen19304%E2%80%939-96)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann19225-100)

[![Image 22](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/GaussSiegel1777-1855.png/250px-GaussSiegel1777-1855.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GaussSiegel1777-1855.png)

Gauss's [seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_/(emblem/) "Seal (emblem)") with his motto _Pauca sed Matura_

Gauss was only willing to publish work when he considered it complete and above criticism. This [perfectionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfectionism_/(psychology/) "Perfectionism (psychology)") was in keeping with the motto of his personal [seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_/(emblem/) "Seal (emblem)") _Pauca sed Matura_ ("Few, but Ripe"). Many colleagues encouraged him to publicize new ideas and sometimes rebuked him if he hesitated too long, in their opinion. Gauss defended himself by claiming that the initial discovery of ideas was easy, but preparing a presentable elaboration was a demanding matter for him, for either lack of time or "serenity of mind".[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Biermann-45) Nevertheless, he published many short communications of urgent content in various journals, but left a considerable literary estate, too.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein197929-101)[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington2004420%E2%80%93430-102) Gauss referred to mathematics as "the queen of sciences" and arithmetics as "the queen of mathematics",[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESartorius_von_Waltershausen185679-103) and supposedly once espoused a belief in the necessity of immediately understanding [Euler's identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_identity "Euler's identity") as a benchmark pursuant to becoming a first-class mathematician.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-First-Class-104)

On certain occasions, Gauss claimed that the ideas of another scholar had already been in his possession previously. Thus his concept of priority as "the first to discover, not the first to publish" differed from that of his scientific contemporaries.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Stigler-105) In contrast to his perfectionism in presenting mathematical ideas, his citations were criticized as negligent. He justified himself with an unusual view of correct citation practice: he would only give complete references, with respect to the previous authors of importance, which no one should ignore, but citing in this way would require knowledge of the history of science and more time than he wished to spend.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Biermann-45)

Soon after Gauss's death, his friend Sartorius published the first biography (1856), written in a rather enthusiastic style. Sartorius saw him as a serene and forward-striving man with childlike modesty,[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESartorius_von_Waltershausen1856102-106) but also of "iron character"[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESartorius_von_Waltershausen185695-107) with an unshakeable strength of mind.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESartorius_von_Waltershausen18568-108) Apart from his closer circle, others regarded him as reserved and unapproachable "like an [Olympian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve_Olympians "Twelve Olympians") sitting enthroned on the summit of science".[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWu%C3%9Fing198241-109) His close contemporaries agreed that Gauss was a man of difficult character. He often refused to accept compliments. His visitors were occasionally irritated by his grumpy behaviour, but a short time later his mood could change, and he would become a charming, open-minded host.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Biermann-45) Gauss disliked polemic natures; together with his colleague [Hausmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Friedrich_Ludwig_Hausmann "Johann Friedrich Ludwig Hausmann") he opposed to a call for [Justus Liebig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justus_Liebig "Justus Liebig") on a university chair in Göttingen, "because he was always involved in some polemic."[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington2004253-110)

[![Image 23](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/G%C3%B6ttingen%2C_Kurze_Stra%C3%9Fe_15%2C_001.jpg/250px-G%C3%B6ttingen%2C_Kurze_Stra%C3%9Fe_15%2C_001.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:G%C3%B6ttingen,_Kurze_Stra%C3%9Fe_15,_001.jpg)

Gauss's residence from 1808 to 1816 in the first floor

Gauss's life was overshadowed by severe problems in his family. When his first wife Johanna suddenly died shortly after the birth of their third child, he revealed the grief in a last letter to his dead wife in the style of an ancient [threnody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threnody "Threnody"), the most personal of his surviving documents.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-111)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington200494%E2%80%9395-112) His second wife and his two daughters suffered from [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis").[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington2004206,_374-113) In a letter to [Bessel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Wilhelm_Bessel "Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel"), dated December 1831, Gauss hinted at his distress, describing himself as "the victim of the worst domestic sufferings".[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Biermann-45)

Because of his wife's illness, both younger sons were educated for some years in [Celle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celle "Celle"), far from Göttingen. The military career of his elder son Joseph ended after more than two decades at the poorly paid rank of [first lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_lieutenant "First lieutenant"), although he had acquired a considerable knowledge of geodesy. He needed financial support from his father even after he was married.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Gerardy-59) The second son Eugen shared a good measure of his father's talent in computation and languages but had a lively and sometimes rebellious character. He wanted to study philology, whereas Gauss wanted him to become a lawyer. Having run up debts and caused a scandal in public,[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-gausschildren-114) Eugen suddenly left Göttingen under dramatic circumstances in September 1830 and emigrated via Bremen to the United States. He wasted the little money he had taken to start, after which his father refused further financial support.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Gerardy-59) The youngest son Wilhelm wanted to qualify for agricultural administration, but had difficulties getting an appropriate education, and eventually emigrated as well. Only Gauss's youngest daughter Therese accompanied him in his last years of life.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington2004374-78)

In his later years Gauss habitually collected various types of useful or useless numerical data, such as the number of paths from his home to certain places in Göttingen or peoples' ages in days; he congratulated [Humboldt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Humboldt "Alexander von Humboldt") in December 1851 for having reached the same age as [Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton "Isaac Newton") at his death, calculated in days.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESartorius_von_Waltershausen185671-115)

Beyond his excellent knowledge of [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin"), he was also acquainted with modern languages. Gauss read both classical and modern literature, and English and French works in the original languages.[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington2004241-116)[\[m\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-118) His favorite English author was [Walter Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Scott "Walter Scott"), his favorite German [Jean Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Paul "Jean Paul"). At the age of 62, he began to teach himself [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"), very likely to understand scientific writings from Russia, among them those of [Lobachevsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Lobachevsky "Nikolai Lobachevsky") on non-Euclidean geometry.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-119)[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWu%C3%9Fing198280-120) Gauss liked singing and went to concerts.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWu%C3%9Fing198281-121) He was a busy newspaper reader; in his last years, he would visit an academic press salon of the university every noon.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESartorius_von_Waltershausen185694-122) Gauss did not care much for philosophy, and mocked the "splitting hairs of the so-called metaphysicians", by which he meant proponents of the contemporary school of _[Naturphilosophie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturphilosophie "Naturphilosophie")_.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWu%C3%9Fing198279-123)

Gauss had an "aristocratic and through and through conservative nature", with little respect for people's intelligence and morals, following the motto "[mundus vult decipi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundus_vult_decipi,_ergo_decipiatur "Mundus vult decipi, ergo decipiatur")".[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESartorius_von_Waltershausen185694-122) He disliked Napoleon and his system and was horrified by violence and revolution of all kinds. Thus he condemned the methods of the [Revolutions of 1848](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1848 "Revolutions of 1848"), though he agreed with some of their aims, such as that of a unified Germany.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESartorius_von_Waltershausen185695-107)[\[n\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-124) He had a low estimation of the constitutional system and he criticized parliamentarians of his time for their perceived ignorance and logical errors.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESartorius_von_Waltershausen185694-122)

Some Gauss biographers have speculated on his religious beliefs. He sometimes said "God arithmetizes"[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESartorius_von_Waltershausen185697-125) and "I succeeded – not on account of my hard efforts, but by the grace of the Lord."[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-126) Gauss was a member of the [Lutheran church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheran_church "Lutheran church"), like most of the population in northern Germany, but it seems that he did not believe all Lutheran [dogma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dogma "Dogma") or understand the Bible fully literally.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington2004300-127) According to Sartorius, Gauss's [religious tolerance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_tolerance "Religious tolerance"), "insatiable thirst for truth" and sense of justice were motivated by his religious convictions.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESartorius_von_Waltershausen1856100-128)

### Algebra and number theory

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Friedrich_Gauss&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Algebra and number theory")\]

#### Fundamental theorem of algebra

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Friedrich_Gauss&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Fundamental theorem of algebra")\]

[![Image 24](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/DBP_1977_928_Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F.jpg/250px-DBP_1977_928_Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DBP_1977_928_Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F.jpg)

German stamp commemorating Gauss's 200th anniversary: the [complex plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_plane "Complex plane") or _Gauss plane_

In his doctoral thesis from 1799, Gauss proved the [fundamental theorem of algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_algebra "Fundamental theorem of algebra") which states that every non-constant single-variable [polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynomial "Polynomial") with complex coefficients has at least one complex [root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_of_a_function "Root of a function"). Mathematicians including [Jean le Rond d'Alembert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_le_Rond_d%27Alembert "Jean le Rond d'Alembert") had produced false proofs before him, and Gauss's dissertation contains a critique of d'Alembert's work. He subsequently produced three other proofs, the last one in 1849 being generally rigorous. His attempts led to considerable clarification of the concept of complex numbers.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-129)

#### _Disquisitiones Arithmeticae_

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Friedrich_Gauss&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae")\]

In the preface to the _Disquisitiones_, Gauss dates the beginning of his work on number theory to 1795. By studying the works of previous mathematicians like Fermat, Euler, Lagrange, and Legendre, he realized that these scholars had already found much of what he had independently discovered.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann19228-130) The _[Disquisitiones Arithmeticae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disquisitiones_Arithmeticae "Disquisitiones Arithmeticae")_, written in 1798 and published in 1801, consolidated number theory as a discipline and covered both elementary and algebraic [number theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number_theory "Number theory"). Therein he introduces the [triple bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_bar "Triple bar") symbol (≡) for [congruence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruence_relation "Congruence relation")[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-131) and uses it for a clean presentation of [modular arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic "Modular arithmetic").[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann19228%E2%80%939-132) It deals with the [unique factorization theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unique_factorization_theorem "Unique factorization theorem") and [primitive roots modulo n](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitive_root_modulo_n "Primitive root modulo n"). In the main sections, Gauss presents the first two proofs of the law of [quadratic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_reciprocity "Quadratic reciprocity")[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann192216%E2%80%9325-133) and develops the theories of [binary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_quadratic_form "Binary quadratic form")[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann192214%E2%80%9316,_25-134) and ternary [quadratic forms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_form "Quadratic form").[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann192225%E2%80%9328-135)

The _Disquisitiones_ include the [Gauss composition law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_composition_law "Gauss composition law") for binary quadratic forms, as well as the enumeration of the number of representations of an integer as the sum of three squares. As an almost immediate corollary of his [theorem on three squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre%27s_three-square_theorem "Legendre's three-square theorem"), he proves the triangular case of the [Fermat polygonal number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_polygonal_number_theorem "Fermat polygonal number theorem") for _n_ = 3.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann192229-136) From several analytic results on [class numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_class_group "Ideal class group") that Gauss gives without proof towards the end of the fifth section,[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann192222%E2%80%9323-137) it appears that Gauss already knew the [class number formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_formula "Class number formula") in 1801.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann192266%E2%80%9369-138)

In the last section, Gauss gives proof for the [constructibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructible_polygon "Constructible polygon") of a regular [heptadecagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heptadecagon "Heptadecagon") (17-sided polygon) with [straightedge and compass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compass_and_straightedge_constructions "Compass and straightedge constructions") by reducing this geometrical problem to an algebraic one.[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Denker-139) This was the first progress in regular polygon construction in over 2000 years.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-140) He shows that a regular polygon is constructible if the number of its sides is either a [power of 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_of_2 "Power of 2") or the product of a power of 2 and any number of distinct [Fermat primes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_prime "Fermat prime"). In the same section, he gives a result on the number of solutions of certain cubic polynomials with coefficients in [finite fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finite_field "Finite field"), which amounts to counting integral points on an [elliptic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_curve "Elliptic curve").[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Stuhler-141) An unfinished chapter, consisting of work done during 1797–1799, was found among his papers after his death.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington200444-142)[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Frei-143)

#### Further investigations

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Friedrich_Gauss&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Further investigations")\]

One of Gauss's first results was the empirically found conjecture of 1792 – the later called [prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem "Prime number theorem") – giving an estimation of the number of prime numbers by using the [integral logarithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logarithmic_integral_function "Logarithmic integral function").[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-144)[\[o\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-146)

In 1816, [Olbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Wilhelm_Matthias_Olbers "Heinrich Wilhelm Matthias Olbers") encouraged Gauss to compete for a prize from the French Academy for a proof for [Fermat's Last Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_Last_Theorem "Fermat's Last Theorem"); he refused, considering the topic uninteresting. However, after his death a short undated paper was found with proofs of the theorem for the cases _n_ = 3 and _n_ = 5.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-147) The particular case of _n_ = 3 was proved much earlier by [Leonhard Euler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonhard_Euler "Leonhard Euler"), but Gauss developed a more streamlined proof which made use of [Eisenstein integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eisenstein_integers "Eisenstein integers"); though more general, the proof was simpler than in the real integers case.[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann192260%E2%80%9361-148)

Gauss contributed to solving the [Kepler conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler_conjecture "Kepler conjecture") in 1831 with the proof that a [greatest packing density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close-packing_of_equal_spheres "Close-packing of equal spheres") of spheres in the three-dimensional space is given when the centres of the spheres form a [cubic face-centred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_crystal_system "Cubic crystal system") arrangement,[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-149) when he reviewed a book of [Ludwig August Seeber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_August_Seeber "Ludwig August Seeber") on the theory of reduction of positive ternary quadratic forms.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-150) Having noticed some lacks in Seeber's proof, he simplified many of his arguments, proved the central conjecture, and remarked that this theorem is equivalent to the Kepler conjecture for regular arrangements.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-151)

In two papers on [biquadratic residues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartic_reciprocity "Quartic reciprocity") (1828, 1832) Gauss introduced the [ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_theory "Ring theory") of [Gaussian integers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_integers "Gaussian integers") ![Image 25: {\displaystyle \mathbb {Z} [i]}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/9ffa94e9e2e6d9e5e5373d5fafb954b902743fde), showed that it is a [unique factorization domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unique_factorization_domain "Unique factorization domain"),[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Kleiner1998-152) and generalized some key arithmetic concepts, such as [Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_little_theorem "Fermat's little theorem") and [Gauss's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_lemma_/(number_theory/) "Gauss's lemma (number theory)"). The main objective of introducing this ring was to formulate the law of biquadratic reciprocity[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Kleiner1998-152) – as Gauss discovered, rings of complex integers are the natural setting for such higher reciprocity laws.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-153)

In the second paper, he stated the general law of biquadratic reciprocity and proved several special cases of it. In an earlier publication from 1818 containing his fifth and sixth proofs of quadratic reciprocity, he claimed the techniques of these proofs ([Gauss sums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_sum "Gauss sum")) can be applied to prove higher reciprocity laws.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBachmann192252,_57%E2%80%9359-154)

One of Gauss's first discoveries was the notion of the [arithmetic-geometric mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic-geometric_mean "Arithmetic-geometric mean") (AGM) of two positive real numbers.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger193341%E2%80%9357-155) He discovered its relation to elliptic integrals in the years 1798–1799 through [Landen's transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landen%27s_transformation "Landen's transformation"), and a diary entry recorded the discovery of the connection of [Gauss's constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_constant "Gauss's constant") to [lemniscatic elliptic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemniscatic_elliptic_functions "Lemniscatic elliptic functions"), a result that Gauss stated "will surely open an entirely new field of analysis".[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Cox-156) He also made early inroads into the more formal issues of the foundations of [complex analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_analysis "Complex analysis"), and from a letter to Bessel in 1811 it is clear that he knew the "fundamental theorem of complex analysis" – [Cauchy's integral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%27s_integral_theorem "Cauchy's integral theorem") – and understood the notion of [complex residues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residue_/(complex_analysis/) "Residue (complex analysis)") when integrating around [poles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pole_/(complex_analysis/) "Pole (complex analysis)").[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Stuhler-141)[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-157)

[Euler's pentagonal numbers theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagonal_number_theorem "Pentagonal number theorem"), together with other researches on the AGM and lemniscatic functions, led him to plenty of results on [Jacobi theta functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_theta_functions "Jacobi theta functions"),[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Stuhler-141) culminating in the discovery in 1808 of the later called [Jacobi triple product identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_triple_product_identity "Jacobi triple product identity"), which includes Euler's theorem as a special case.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-158) His works show that he knew modular transformations of order 3, 5, 7 for elliptic functions since 1808.[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger1933185%E2%80%93186-159)[\[p\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-160)[\[q\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-162)

Several mathematical fragments in his [Nachlass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nachlass "Nachlass") indicate that he knew parts of the modern theory of [modular forms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_forms "Modular forms").[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Stuhler-141) In his work on the [multivalued](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivalued_function "Multivalued function") AGM of two complex numbers, he discovered a deep connection between the infinitely many values of the AGM and its two "simplest values".[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Cox-156) In his unpublished writings he recognized and made a sketch of the key concept of [fundamental domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_domain "Fundamental domain") for the [modular group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_group "Modular group").[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger1933101%E2%80%93106-163)[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Houzel-164) One of Gauss's sketches of this kind was a drawing of a [tessellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tessellation "Tessellation") of the [unit disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_disk "Unit disk") by "equilateral" [hyperbolic triangles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_triangle "Hyperbolic triangle") with all angles equal to ![Image 26: {\displaystyle \pi /4}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/1707aa0fec2c8ef008b9e30b6045fbf95dab9e20).[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-165)

An example of Gauss's insight in analysis is the cryptic remark that the principles of circle division by compass and straightedge can also be applied to the division of the [lemniscate curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemniscate_curve "Lemniscate curve"), which inspired Abel's theorem on lemniscate division.[\[r\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-166) Another example is his publication "Summatio quarundam serierum singularium" (1811) on the determination of the sign of [quadratic Gauss sums](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Quadratic_Gauss_sums&action=edit&redlink=1 "Quadratic Gauss sums (page does not exist)"), in which he solved the main problem by introducing [q-analogs of binomial coefficients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_binomial_coefficient "Gaussian binomial coefficient") and manipulating them by several original identities that seem to stem from his work on elliptic function theory; however, Gauss cast his argument in a formal way that does not reveal its origin in elliptic function theory, and only the later work of mathematicians such as [Jacobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Gustav_Jacob_Jacobi "Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi") and [Hermite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermite "Hermite") has exposed the crux of his argument.[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger1933122%E2%80%93123-167)

In the "Disquisitiones generales circa series infinitam..." (1813), he provides the first systematic treatment of the general [hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function "Hypergeometric function") ![Image 27: {\displaystyle F(\alpha ,\beta ,\gamma ,x)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f479aea7571b5ea41a92cbfa38a8f51826ea8471), and shows that many of the functions known at the time are special cases of the hypergeometric function.[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger1933136%E2%80%93142-168) This work is the first exact inquiry into [convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergent_series "Convergent series") of infinite series in the history of mathematics.[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger1933142-169) Furthermore, it deals with infinite [continued fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continued_fraction "Continued fraction") arising as ratios of hypergeometric functions, which are now called [Gauss continued fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_continued_fraction "Gauss continued fraction").[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger1933136%E2%80%93154-170)

In 1823, Gauss won the prize of the Danish Society with an essay on [conformal mappings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conformal_mapping "Conformal mapping"), which contains several developments that pertain to the field of complex analysis.[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt%C3%A4ckel191790%E2%80%9391-171) Gauss stated that angle-preserving mappings in the complex plane must be complex [analytic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytic_function "Analytic function"), and used the later-named [Beltrami equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beltrami_equation "Beltrami equation") to prove the existence of [isothermal coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isothermal_coordinates "Isothermal coordinates") on analytic surfaces. The essay concludes with examples of conformal mappings into a sphere and an [ellipsoid of revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipsoid_of_revolution "Ellipsoid of revolution").[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%BChler1981103-172)

Gauss often deduced theorems [inductively](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inductive_reasoning "Inductive reasoning") from numerical data he had collected empirically.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger193318-94) As such, the use of efficient algorithms to facilitate calculations was vital to his research, and he made many contributions to [numerical analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_analysis "Numerical analysis"), such as the method of [Gaussian quadrature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_quadrature "Gaussian quadrature"), published in 1816.[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-173)

In a private letter to [Gerling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Ludwig_Gerling "Christian Ludwig Gerling") from 1823,[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-174) he described a solution of a 4x4 system of linear equations with the [Gauss-Seidel method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss-Seidel_method "Gauss-Seidel method") – an "indirect" [iterative method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterative_method "Iterative method") for the solution of linear systems, and recommended it over the usual method of "direct elimination" for systems of more than two equations.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-175)

Gauss invented an algorithm for calculating what is now called [discrete Fourier transforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_Fourier_transform "Discrete Fourier transform") when calculating the orbits of Pallas and Juno in 1805, 160 years before [Cooley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cooley "James Cooley") and [Tukey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tukey "John Tukey") found their similar [Cooley–Tukey algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooley-Tukey_FFT_algorithm "Cooley-Tukey FFT algorithm").[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-176) He developed it as a [trigonometric interpolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_interpolation "Trigonometric interpolation") method, but the paper _Theoria Interpolationis Methodo Nova Tractata_ was published only posthumously in 1876,[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-177) well after [Joseph Fourier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Fourier "Joseph Fourier")'s introduction of the subject in 1807.[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-178)

#### Differential geometry

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Friedrich_Gauss&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Differential geometry")\]

The geodetic survey of [Hanover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanover "Hanover") fuelled Gauss's interest in [differential geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry "Differential geometry") and [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology "Topology"), fields of mathematics dealing with [curves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve "Curve") and [surfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface_/(topology/) "Surface (topology)"). This led him in 1828 to the publication of a work that marks the birth of modern [differential geometry of surfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_geometry_of_surfaces "Differential geometry of surfaces"), as it departed from the traditional ways of treating surfaces as [cartesian graphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_coordinate_system "Cartesian coordinate system") of functions of two variables, and that initiated the exploration of surfaces from the "inner" point of view of a two-dimensional being constrained to move on it. As a result, the [Theorema Egregium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorema_Egregium "Theorema Egregium") (_remarkable theorem_), established a property of the notion of [Gaussian curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_curvature "Gaussian curvature"). Informally, the theorem says that the curvature of a surface can be determined entirely by measuring [angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle "Angle") and [distances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance "Distance") on the surface, regardless of the [embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embedding "Embedding") of the surface in three-dimensional or two-dimensional space.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt%C3%A4ckel1917110%E2%80%93119-179)

The Theorema Egregium leads to the abstraction of surfaces as doubly-extended [manifolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifold "Manifold"); it clarifies the distinction between the intrinsic properties of the manifold (the [metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_tensor "Metric tensor")) and its physical realization in ambient space. A consequence is the impossibility of an isometric transformation between surfaces of different Gaussian curvature. This means practically that a [sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere "Sphere") or an [ellipsoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellipsoid "Ellipsoid") cannot be transformed to a plane without distortion, which causes a fundamental problem in designing [projections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Map_projection "Map projection") for geographical maps.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt%C3%A4ckel1917110%E2%80%93119-179) A portion of this essay is dedicated to a profound study of [geodesics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic "Geodesic"). In particular, Gauss proves the local [Gauss–Bonnet theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Bonnet_theorem "Gauss–Bonnet theorem") on geodesic triangles, and generalizes [Legendre's theorem on spherical triangles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre%27s_theorem_on_spherical_triangles "Legendre's theorem on spherical triangles") to geodesic triangles on arbitrary surfaces with continuous curvature; he found that the angles of a "sufficiently small" geodesic triangle deviate from that of a planar triangle of the same sides in a way that depends only on the values of the surface curvature at the vertices of the triangle, regardless of the behaviour of the surface in the triangle interior.[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt%C3%A4ckel1917105%E2%80%93106-180)

Gauss's memoir from 1828 lacks the conception of [geodesic curvature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesic_curvature "Geodesic curvature"). However, in a previously unpublished manuscript, very likely written in 1822–1825, he introduced the term "side curvature" (German: "Seitenkrümmung") and proved its [invariance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invariant_/(mathematics/) "Invariant (mathematics)") under isometric transformations, a result that was later obtained by [Ferdinand Minding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Minding "Ferdinand Minding") and published by him in 1830. This Gauss paper contains the core of his lemma on total curvature, but also its generalization, found and proved by [Pierre Ossian Bonnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Ossian_Bonnet "Pierre Ossian Bonnet") in 1848 and known as the [Gauss–Bonnet theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Bonnet_theorem "Gauss–Bonnet theorem").[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBolza192170%E2%80%9374-181)

#### Non-Euclidean geometry

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Friedrich_Gauss&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Non-Euclidean geometry")\]

[![Image 28](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Bendixen_-_Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F%2C_1828.jpg/250px-Bendixen_-_Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F%2C_1828.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bendixen_-_Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F,_1828.jpg)

Lithograph of Gauss by [Siegfried Bendixen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegfried_Bendixen "Siegfried Bendixen") (1828)

During Gauss's lifetime, the [parallel postulate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_postulate "Parallel postulate") of [Euclidean geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_geometry "Euclidean geometry") was heavily discussed.[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt%C3%A4ckel191719%E2%80%9320-182) Numerous efforts were made to prove it in the frame of the Euclidean [axioms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom "Axiom"), whereas some mathematicians discussed the possibility of geometrical systems without it.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%BChler1981100%E2%80%93102-183) Gauss thought about the basics of geometry from the 1790s on, but only realized in the 1810s that a non-Euclidean geometry without the parallel postulate could solve the problem.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein197957%E2%80%9360-184)[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt%C3%A4ckel191719%E2%80%9320-182) In a letter to [Franz Taurinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Taurinus "Franz Taurinus") of 1824, he presented a short comprehensible outline of what he named a "[non-Euclidean geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Euclidean_geometry "Non-Euclidean geometry")",[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-:0-185) but he strongly forbade Taurinus to make any use of it.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein197957%E2%80%9360-184) Gauss is credited with having been the one to first discover and study non-Euclidean geometry, even coining the term as well.[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-186)[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-:0-185)[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-187)

The first publications on non-Euclidean geometry in the history of mathematics were authored by [Nikolai Lobachevsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Lobachevsky "Nikolai Lobachevsky") in 1829 and [Janos Bolyai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janos_Bolyai "Janos Bolyai") in 1832.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%BChler1981100%E2%80%93102-183) In the following years, Gauss wrote his ideas on the topic but did not publish them, thus avoiding influencing the contemporary scientific discussion.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein197957%E2%80%9360-184)[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-188) Gauss commended the ideas of Janos Bolyai in a letter to his father and university friend Farkas Bolyai[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-189) claiming that these were congruent to his own thoughts of some decades.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein197957%E2%80%9360-184)[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-190) However, it is not quite clear to what extent he preceded Lobachevsky and Bolyai, as his written remarks are vague and obscure.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEB%C3%BChler1981100%E2%80%93102-183)

[Sartorius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Sartorius_von_Waltershausen "Wolfgang Sartorius von Waltershausen") first mentioned Gauss's work on non-Euclidean geometry in 1856, but only the publication of Gauss's [Nachlass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nachlass "Nachlass") in Volume VIII of the Collected Works (1900) showed Gauss's ideas on the matter, at a time when non-Euclidean geometry was still an object of some controversy.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein197957%E2%80%9360-184)

Gauss was also an early pioneer of [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology "Topology") or _Geometria Situs_, as it was called in his lifetime. The first proof of the [fundamental theorem of algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_theorem_of_algebra "Fundamental theorem of algebra") in 1799 contained an essentially topological argument; fifty years later, he further developed the topological argument in his fourth proof of this theorem.[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOstrowski19201%E2%80%9318-191)

[![Image 29](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F%2C_B%C3%BCste_von_Heinrich_Hesemann%2C_1855.jpg/250px-Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F%2C_B%C3%BCste_von_Heinrich_Hesemann%2C_1855.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F,_B%C3%BCste_von_Heinrich_Hesemann,_1855.jpg)

Gauss bust by Heinrich Hesemann (1855)[\[s\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-192)

Another encounter with topological notions occurred to him in the course of his astronomical work in 1804, when he determined the limits of the region on the [celestial sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_sphere "Celestial sphere") in which comets and asteroids might appear, and which he termed "Zodiacus". He discovered that if the Earth's and comet's orbits are [linked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Link_/(knot_theory/) "Link (knot theory)"), then by topological reasons the Zodiacus is the entire sphere. In 1848, in the context of the discovery of the asteroid [7 Iris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_Iris "7 Iris"), he published a further qualitative discussion of the Zodiacus.[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Epple_1998_45%E2%80%9352-193)

In Gauss's letters of 1820–1830, he thought intensively on topics with close affinity to Geometria Situs, and became gradually conscious of semantic difficulty in this field. Fragments from this period reveal that he tried to classify "tract figures", which are closed plane curves with a finite number of transverse self-intersections, that may also be planar projections of [knots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knot_theory "Knot theory").[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-194) To do so he devised a symbolical scheme, the [Gauss code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_code "Gauss code"), that in a sense captured the characteristic features of tract figures.[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-195)[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt%C3%A4ckel191750%E2%80%9351-196)

In a fragment from 1833, Gauss defined the [linking number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linking_number "Linking number") of two space curves by a certain double integral, and in doing so provided for the first time an analytical formulation of a topological phenomenon. On the same note, he lamented the little progress made in Geometria Situs, and remarked that one of its central problems will be "to count the intertwinings of two closed or infinite curves". His notebooks from that period reveal that he was also thinking about other topological objects such as [braids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braid_theory "Braid theory") and [tangles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangle_/(mathematics/) "Tangle (mathematics)").[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Epple_1998_45%E2%80%9352-193)

Gauss's influence in later years to the emerging field of topology, which he held in high esteem, was through occasional remarks and oral communications to Mobius and Listing.[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt%C3%A4ckel191751%E2%80%9355-197)

### Minor mathematical accomplishments

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Friedrich_Gauss&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Minor mathematical accomplishments")\]

Gauss applied the concept of complex numbers to solve well-known problems in a new concise way. For example, in a short note from 1836 on geometric aspects of the ternary forms and their application to crystallography,[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-198) he stated the [fundamental theorem of axonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axonometry "Axonometry"), which tells how to represent a 3D cube on a 2D plane with complete accuracy, via complex numbers.[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-199) He described rotations of this sphere as the action of certain [linear fractional transformations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobius_transformation "Mobius transformation") on the extended complex plane,[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger1933198-200) and gave a proof for the geometric theorem that the [altitudes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude_/(triangle/) "Altitude (triangle)") of a triangle always meet in a single [orthocenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthocenter "Orthocenter").[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-201)

Gauss was concerned with [John Napier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Napier "John Napier")'s "[Pentagramma mirificum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagramma_mirificum "Pentagramma mirificum")" – a certain spherical [pentagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagram "Pentagram") – for several decades;[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-202) he approached it from various points of view, and gradually gained a full understanding of its geometric, algebraic, and analytic aspects.[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-203) In particular, in 1843 he stated and proved several theorems connecting elliptic functions, Napier spherical pentagons, and Poncelet pentagons in the plane.[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-204)

Furthermore, he contributed a solution to the problem of constructing the largest-area ellipse inside a given [quadrilateral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadrilateral "Quadrilateral"),[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-205)[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt%C3%A4ckel191771-72-206) and discovered a surprising result about the computation of area of [pentagons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentagon "Pentagon").[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-207)[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESt%C3%A4ckel191776-208)

[![Image 30](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F%2C_Pastellgem%C3%A4lde_von_Johann_Christian_August_Schwartz%2C_1803%2C_ohne_Rahmen.jpg/250px-Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F%2C_Pastellgem%C3%A4lde_von_Johann_Christian_August_Schwartz%2C_1803%2C_ohne_Rahmen.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carl_Friedrich_Gau%C3%9F,_Pastellgem%C3%A4lde_von_Johann_Christian_August_Schwartz,_1803,_ohne_Rahmen.jpg)

Carl Friedrich Gauss 1803 by Johann Christian August Schwartz

On 1 January 1801, Italian astronomer [Giuseppe Piazzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Piazzi "Giuseppe Piazzi") discovered a new celestial object, presumed it to be the long searched planet between Mars and Jupiter according to the so-called [Titius–Bode law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titius%E2%80%93Bode_law "Titius–Bode law"), and named it [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_/(dwarf_planet/) "Ceres (dwarf planet)").[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-209) He could track it only for a short time until it disappeared behind the glare of the Sun. The mathematical tools of the time were not sufficient to predict the location of its reappearance from the few data available. Gauss tackled the problem and predicted a position for possible rediscovery in December 1801. This turned out to be accurate within a half-degree when [Franz Xaver von Zach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Xaver_von_Zach "Franz Xaver von Zach") on 7 and 31 December at [Gotha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gotha_Observatory "Gotha Observatory"), and independently [Heinrich Olbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Wilhelm_Matth%C3%A4us_Olbers "Heinrich Wilhelm Matthäus Olbers") on 1 and 2 January in [Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bremen "Bremen"), identified the object near the predicted position.[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-210)[\[t\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-211)

[Gauss's method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_method "Gauss's method") leads to an equation of the eighth degree, of which one solution, the Earth's orbit, is known. The solution sought is then separated from the remaining six based on physical conditions. In this work, Gauss used comprehensive approximation methods which he created for that purpose.[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlein19798-212)

The discovery of Ceres led Gauss to the theory of the motion of planetoids disturbed by large planets, eventually published in 1809 as _Theoria motus corporum coelestium in sectionibus conicis solem ambientum_.[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-213) It introduced the [Gaussian gravitational constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_gravitational_constant "Gaussian gravitational constant").[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Wittmann-41)

Since the new asteroids had been discovered, Gauss occupied himself with the [perturbations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perturbation_/(astronomy/) "Perturbation (astronomy)") of their [orbital elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_elements "Orbital elements"). Firstly he examined Ceres with analytical methods similar to those of Laplace, but his favorite object was [Pallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki//(2/)_Pallas "(2) Pallas"), because of its great [eccentricity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eccentricity_/(astronomy/) "Eccentricity (astronomy)") and [orbital inclination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_inclination "Orbital inclination"), whereby Laplace's method did not work. Gauss used his own tools: the [arithmetic–geometric mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic%E2%80%93geometric_mean "Arithmetic–geometric mean"), the [hypergeometric function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypergeometric_function "Hypergeometric function"), and his method of interpolation.[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrendel1929194%E2%80%93195-214) He found an [orbital resonance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_resonance#Coincidental_'near'_ratios_of_mean_motion "Orbital resonance") with [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter") in proportion 18:7 in 1812; Gauss gave this result as [cipher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cipher "Cipher"), and gave the explicit meaning only in letters to Olbers and Bessel.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrendel1929206-215)[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-216)[\[u\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-218) After long years of work, he finished it in 1816 without a result that seemed sufficient to him. This marked the end of his activities in theoretical astronomy.[\[198\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrendel1929254-219)

[![Image 31](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Goettingen_Sternwarte_Besemann.png/250px-Goettingen_Sternwarte_Besemann.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Goettingen_Sternwarte_Besemann.png)

Göttingen observatory seen from the North-west (by Friedrich Besemann, c. 1835)

One fruit of Gauss's research on Pallas perturbations was the _Determinatio Attractionis..._ (1818) on a method of theoretical astronomy that later became known as the "elliptic ring method". It introduced an averaging conception in which a planet in orbit is replaced by a fictitious ring with mass density proportional to the time the planet takes to follow the corresponding orbital arcs.[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrendel1929253%E2%80%93254-220) Gauss presents the method of evaluating the gravitational attraction of such an elliptic ring, which includes several steps; one of them involves a direct application of the arithmetic-geometric mean (AGM) algorithm to calculate an [elliptic integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_integral "Elliptic integral").[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchlesinger1933169%E2%80%93170-221)

Even after Gauss's contributions to theoretical astronomy came to an end, more practical activities in [observational astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observational_astronomy "Observational astronomy") continued and occupied him during his entire career. As early as 1799, Gauss dealt with the determination of longitude by use of the lunar parallax, for which he developed more convenient formulas than those were in common use.[\[201\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrendel19298%E2%80%939-222) After appointment as director of observatory he attached importance to the fundamental astronomical constants in correspondence with Bessel. Gauss himself provided tables of [nutation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_nutation "Astronomical nutation") and [aberration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberration_/(astronomy/) "Aberration (astronomy)"), solar coordinates, and refraction.[\[202\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrendel19293-223) He made many contributions to [spherical geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spherical_geometry "Spherical geometry"), and in this context solved some practical problems about [navigation by stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celestial_navigation "Celestial navigation").[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrendel192954-224) He published a great number of observations, mainly on minor planets and comets; his last observation was the [solar eclipse of 28 July 1851](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Solar_eclipse_of_28_July_1851&action=edit&redlink=1 "Solar eclipse of 28 July 1851 (page does not exist)").[\[204\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrendel1929144-225)

Gauss's first publication following his doctoral thesis dealt with the determination of the [date of Easter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Date_of_Easter#Gauss's_Easter_algorithm "Date of Easter") (1800), an elementary mathematical topic. Gauss aimed to present a convenient algorithm for people without any knowledge of ecclesiastical or even astronomical chronology, and thus avoided the usual terms of [golden number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_number_/(time/) "Golden number (time)"), [epact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epact "Epact"), [solar cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cycle_/(calendar/) "Solar cycle (calendar)"), [domenical letter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominical_letter "Dominical letter"), and any religious connotations.[\[205\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMaennchen193049%E2%80%9363-226) This choice of topic likely had historical grounds. The replacement of the [Julian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_calendar "Julian calendar") by the [Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar "Gregorian calendar") had caused confusion in the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") since the 16th century and was not finished in Germany until 1700, when the difference of eleven days was deleted. Even after this, Easter fell on different dates in Protestant and Catholic territories, until this difference was abolished by agreement in 1776. In the Protestant states, such as the Duchy of Brunswick, the Easter of 1777, five weeks before Gauss's birth, was the first one calculated in the new manner.[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Olesko-227)

Gauss likely used the [method of least squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Least_squares "Least squares") to minimize the impact of [measurement error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observational_error "Observational error") when calculating the orbit of Ceres.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Stigler-105) The method was published first by [Adrien-Marie Legendre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrien-Marie_Legendre "Adrien-Marie Legendre") in 1805, but Gauss claimed in _Theoria motus_ (1809) that he had been using it since 1794 or 1795.[\[207\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchaaf196484-228)[\[208\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-:3-229)[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-230) In the history of statistics, this disagreement is called the "priority dispute over the discovery of the method of least squares".[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Stigler-105) Gauss proved that the method has the lowest sampling variance within the class of linear unbiased estimators under the assumption of [normally distributed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution "Normal distribution") errors ([Gauss–Markov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Markov_theorem "Gauss–Markov theorem")), in the two-part paper _Theoria combinationis observationum erroribus minimis obnoxiae_ (1823).[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-231)

In the first paper he proved [Gauss's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_inequality "Gauss's inequality") (a [Chebyshev-type inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev%27s_inequality "Chebyshev's inequality")) for [unimodal distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimodality "Unimodality"), and stated without proof another inequality for [moments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_/(mathematics/) "Moment (mathematics)") of the fourth order (a special case of the Gauss-Winckler inequality).[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-232) He derived lower and upper bounds for the [variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variance "Variance") of the [sample variance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sample_variance "Sample variance"). In the second paper, Gauss described [recursive least squares methods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recursive_least_squares_filter "Recursive least squares filter"), which he discovered.[\[212\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-233) Gauss's work on the theory of errors was extended in several directions by the geodesist [Friedrich Robert Helmert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Robert_Helmert "Friedrich Robert Helmert") to the [Gauss-Helmert model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss-Helmert_model "Gauss-Helmert model").[\[213\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-234)

Gauss also contributed to problems in [probability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_theory "Probability theory") that are not directly concerned with the theory of errors. One example appears as a diary note where he tried to describe the asymptotic distribution of entries in the continued fraction expansion of a random number uniformly distributed in _(0,1)_. He derived this distribution, now known as the [Gauss-Kuzmin distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss-Kuzmin_distribution "Gauss-Kuzmin distribution"), as a by-product of the discovery of the [ergodicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergodicity "Ergodicity") of the [Gauss map for continued fractions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss-Kuzmin-Wirsing_operator "Gauss-Kuzmin-Wirsing operator"). Gauss's solution is the first-ever result in the metrical theory of continued fractions.[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-235)

Gauss was busy with geodetic problems since 1799 when he helped [Karl Ludwig von Lecoq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Ludwig_von_Lecoq "Karl Ludwig von Lecoq") with calculations during his [survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveying "Surveying") in [Westphalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westphalia "Westphalia").[\[215\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalle192416%E2%80%9318-236) Beginning in 1804, he taught himself some practical geodesy in Brunswick[\[216\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalle192422-237) and Göttingen.[\[217\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalle192428-238)

Since 1816, Gauss's former student [Heinrich Christian Schumacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Christian_Schumacher "Heinrich Christian Schumacher"), then professor in [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen"), but living in [Altona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altona,_Hamburg "Altona, Hamburg") ([Holstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Holstein "Duchy of Holstein")) near [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg") as head of an observatory, carried out a [triangulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulation "Triangulation") of the [Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutland "Jutland") peninsula from [Skagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skagen "Skagen") in the north to [Lauenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauenburg "Lauenburg") in the south.[\[v\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-239) This project was the basis for map production but also aimed at determining the geodetic arc between the terminal sites. Data from geodetic arcs were used to determine the dimensions of the earth [geoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoid "Geoid"), and long arc distances brought more precise results. Schumacher asked Gauss to continue this work further to the south in the Kingdom of Hanover; Gauss agreed after a short time of hesitation. Finally, in May 1820, King [George IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_IV "George IV") gave the order to Gauss.[\[218\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalle192432-240)

An [arc measurement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_measurement "Arc measurement") needs a precise astronomical determination of at least two points in the [network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulation_network "Triangulation network"). Gauss and Schumacher used the coincidence that both observatories in Göttingen and Altona, in the garden of Schumacher's house, lay nearly in the same [longitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longitude "Longitude"). The [latitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latitude "Latitude") was measured with both their instruments and a [zenith sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zenith_sector "Zenith sector") of [Ramsden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Ramsden "Jesse Ramsden") that was transported to both observatories.[\[219\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalle192461-241)[\[w\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-242)

Gauss and Schumacher had already determined some angles between [Lüneburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCneburg "Lüneburg"), Hamburg, and Lauenburg for the geodetic connection in October 1818.[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalle192460-243) During the summers of 1821 until 1825 Gauss directed the triangulation work personally, from [Thuringia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thuringia "Thuringia") in the south to the river [Elbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elbe "Elbe") in the north. The [triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangle "Triangle") between [Hoher Hagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoher_Hagen_/(Dransfeld/) "Hoher Hagen (Dransfeld)"), [Großer Inselsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gro%C3%9Fer_Inselsberg "Großer Inselsberg") in the [Thuringian Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thuringian_Forest "Thuringian Forest"), and [Brocken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brocken "Brocken") in the [Harz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harz "Harz") mountains was the largest one Gauss had ever measured with a maximum size of 107 km (66.5 miles). In the thinly populated [Lüneburg Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BCneburg_Heath "Lüneburg Heath") without significant natural summits or artificial buildings, he had difficulties finding suitable triangulation points; sometimes cutting lanes through the vegetation was necessary.[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Olesko-227)[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalle192475%E2%80%9380-244)

For pointing signals, Gauss invented a new instrument with movable mirrors and a small telescope that reflects the sunbeams to the triangulation points, and named it _[heliotrope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliotrope_/(instrument/) "Heliotrope (instrument)")_.[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchaaf196481-245) Another suitable construction for the same purpose was a [sextant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sextant "Sextant") with an additional mirror which he named _vice heliotrope_.[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalle192469-246) Gauss was assisted by soldiers of the Hanoverian army, among them his eldest son Joseph. Gauss took part in the [baseline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseline_/(surveying/) "Baseline (surveying)") measurement ([Braak Base Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braak_Base_Line "Braak Base Line")) of Schumacher in the village of [Braak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braak,_Schleswig-Holstein "Braak, Schleswig-Holstein") near Hamburg in 1820, and used the result for the evaluation of the Hanoverian triangulation.[\[224\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington2004121-247)

An additional result was a better value for the [flattening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flattening "Flattening") of the approximative [Earth ellipsoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_ellipsoid "Earth ellipsoid").[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalle192437%E2%80%9338,_49%E2%80%9350-248)[\[x\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-250) Gauss developed the [universal transverse Mercator projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transverse_Mercator_projection#Ellipsoidal_transverse_Mercator "Transverse Mercator projection") of the ellipsoidal shaped Earth (what he named _conform projection_)[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington2004164-251) for representing geodetical data in plane charts.

When the arc measurement was finished, Gauss began the enlargement of the triangulation to the west to get a survey of the whole [Kingdom of Hanover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hanover "Kingdom of Hanover") with a Royal decree from 25 March 1828.[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDunnington2004135-252) The practical work was directed by three army officers, among them Lieutenant Joseph Gauss. The complete data evaluation laid in the hands of Gauss, who applied his mathematical inventions such as the [method of least squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_of_least_squares "Method of least squares") and the [elimination method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_elimination "Gaussian elimination") to it. The project was finished in 1844, and Gauss sent a final report of the project to the government; his method of projection was not edited until 1866.[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGalle1924129-253)[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-254)

In 1828, when studying differences in [latitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latitude "Latitude"), Gauss first defined a physical approximation for the [figure of the Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure_of_the_Earth "Figure of the Earth") as the surface everywhere perpendicular to the direction of gravity;[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-Gau%C3%9F1828-255) later his doctoral student [Johann Benedict Listing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Benedict_Listing "Johann Benedict Listing") called this the _[geoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoid "Geoid")_.[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss#cite_note-256)

### Magnetism and telegraphy

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Friedrich_Gauss&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Magnetism and telegraphy")\]
